extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century readers; gentlemen and readers interested in social conduct, manners, and practical moral advice (also useful to writers depicting social scenes)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and norms for composing and presenting observational, moralizing essays and portraits of social life (e.g., levées, conversation, friendship, temperance), emphasizing conduct, tone, and practical rules for behaviour and argument. Useful for writers depicting manners, or for those seeking prescriptive rules for social interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of a great Man's Levée (market for preferment)
rubrics_metrics.description: An extended description of the Levée as a staged market where the mighty receive acknowledgments that they are 'Wise, Bounteous, Valiant and Powerful' and where a network of porters, valets, and whispers prepares the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the theatrical mechanics (secret signals, ropes/bells analogy), the crowd's ritual bows and civilities, and the Levée's purpose as a public display of deference and preferment. Use this model to depict ceremonial social gatherings: show orchestration (porters/valets), the patron's central position, and the repetitive, farcical exchange of acknowledgments rather than substantive business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep in generals; be in haste with particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief Point is to keep in Generals, and if there be any thing offered that's Particular, to be in haste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a rule for a patron's answers: give broad, general responses to many petitioners; avoid detailed engagement. When particulars arise, dispose of them quickly. For writers: portray powerful figures as masterful in generalities, evasive or hurried when specifics threaten to slow ceremony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid outward show; prioritize real happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Outward Show is what most Men pursue, rather than real Happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of vanity and courtship of appearances: useful as a moral axis in essays — contrast characters who chase display with those who seek substantive pleasures. Use examples of people volunteering servile politeness for social recognition to reveal hollowness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of first appearance (military vs civil)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several Ways of making this first Appearance: you may be either half dressed, and washing your self, which is indeed the most stately... this Way of Opening is peculiar to Military Men... the close Minister is buttoned up, and the brave Officer open-breasted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use differences in ceremonial dress/gesture to signal professional temperament: military characters accept ostentatious vulnerability; civil/political characters prefer reserve and chastity of deportment. Small physical details in an opening scene can convey class, office, and habitual conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of servility and the farce of public deference
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole seems to be a Conspiracy of a Set of Servile Slaves, to give up their own Liberty to take away their Patron's Understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing social satire, depict both idol and idolater as mutually deceiving, each seeking imaginative pleasure from ceremony. Show how submission degrades clients and inflates patrons, making the Levée essentially theatrical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance as a primary preservative of health
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperance... is a kind of Regimen into which every Man may put himself, without Interruption to Business, Expence of Money, or Loss of Time. If Exercise throws off all Superfluities, Temperance prevents them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat temperance as a practical, universally available remedy: contrast it with exercise and with medical interventions used by the idle or intemperate. For essays on health or character, use temperance to dramatize moral as well as physical improvement; illustrate with examples (e.g., Cornaro, Socrates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diet rule: make your whole repast out of one dish; avoid sauces and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your whole Repast out of one Dish. If you indulge in a second, avoid drinking any thing Strong, till you have finished your Meal; at the same time abstain from all Sauces, or at least such as are not the most plain and simple.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical prescription for avoiding gluttony: single-dish meals reduce variety-driven excess and artificial stimulants. Writers giving prescriptive advice should include these concrete, memorable rules (one-dish meal; defer strong drink until after finishing; minimal sauces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for drinking
rubrics_metrics.description: The first Glass for my self, the second for my Friends, the third for good Humour, and the fourth for mine Enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A compact, memorable maxim (attributed to Sir William Temple) to regulate drinking: use such aphorisms to convey moderation and social framing of consumption in essays or character dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt days of abstinence
rubrics_metrics.description: Every Man should have his Days of Abstinence, according as his Constitution will permit. These are great Reliefs to Nature... often kills a Sickness in Embryo, and destroys the first Seeds of an Indisposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend periodic fasting as both preventative and restorative. In prescriptive discourse, stress tailoring to constitution and the health benefits (resilience to hunger/thirst, aborting incipient sickness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance must be adapted to individual constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to lay down any determinate Rule for Temperance, because what is Luxury in one may be Temperance in another; but there are few that have lived any time in the World, who are not Judges of their own Constitutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel against rigid one-size-fits-all rules: encourage self-knowledge and personal moderation. As a writing principle, advise nuanced prescriptions and caveats rather than dogma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek ease and tranquillity rather than absolute happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of presuming to be happy, instruct us only to be easy. The great Lesson is Æquanimity, a Regularity of Spirit, which is a little above Chearfulness and below Mirth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote attainable goals (calm, regular cheerfulness) in moral instruction. For character and thematic work, emphasize domestic comforts, simplicity, industry and temperance as paths to tranquillity rather than grand philosophical felicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disputes; aim to improve not contradict
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid Disputes as much as possible. ... it requires more Wit, as well as more good Humour, to improve than to contradict the Notions of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule for conversation: prefer constructive additions to mere contradiction. For dialogue and social guidance, show characters improving others' ideas with coolness, which is considered more admirable than combative disputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: When obliged to argue, use coolness, modesty, and non-dogmatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Give your Reasons with the utmost Coolness and Modesty... if you are neither Dogmatical, nor shew either by your Actions or Words, that you are full of your self, all will the more heartily rejoice at your Victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument-style rubric: calm tone, humility, and restraint increase persuasiveness and social esteem. The Socratic way—asking questions and soliciting information—prevents being caught in absurdity and preserves good humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the other's biases and education; do not be angry at differing opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Interests, Education, and Means by which Men attain their Knowledge, are so very different, that it is impossible they should all think alike; and he has at least as much Reason to be angry with you, as you with him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imaginative role-taking (ask what your opinion would be under their biases) to temper anger. For writers: portray disputes where characters exercise empathy and self-questioning rather than wrath.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for information, moderate victories; act as moderator
rubrics_metrics.description: If you propose to your self the true End of Argument, which is Information, 'twill be almost indifferent to you where you find it... nothing procures a Man more Esteem and less Envy from the whole Company, than if he chooses the Part of Moderator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame argumentation as collaborative truth-seeking rather than competition. Encourage the role of moderator: impartial sifting of matters, complimenting both sides, and not pressing a victory too far. In composition, depict such moderation as socially admirable and effective.
